title: Ukraine fires its largest-ever drone barrage at Moscow on the final day of Russia's election
summary: Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, hitting the Moscow refinery on the last day of parliamentary voting, while Washington signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law and a Greenland security deal moved to signature at the UN. The Houthis fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh and Germany voted in state elections that will test Chancellor Merz.

stories.headline: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says
stories.dek: The overnight barrage, the biggest on the Russian capital of the war so far, landed on the final day of Russia's parliamentary election and damaged the Moscow oil refinery.
tldr: Ukrainian forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds toward Moscow; Moscow's mayor called it the largest-ever attack on the capital, according to wire reports.

Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones were downed en route to the city and that a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building were damaged; the Moscow region governor reported two dead and 20 wounded.
The attack came on the third and final day of Russia's parliamentary election, which the Kremlin framed as a test of support for the war.

body.text: Ukrainian forces launched one of the largest aerial attacks of the war against the Russian capital overnight into Sunday, with officials in Moscow saying more than 1,000 drones were fired at Russia in total and hundreds directed at the capital. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin described it as the largest-ever drone attack on the city and said an oil refinery and a residential building were hit.

Sobyanin said 450 drones had been destroyed en route to Moscow. The governor of the wider Moscow region, Andrei Vorobyov, reported two people killed and 20 wounded, including three children, in the overnight attacks, according to wire reporting. Ukraine's president said domestically produced long-range drones and missiles were used against oil and logistics facilities, framing the strikes as pressure on the revenue that funds Russia's war machine.

The timing was pointed: the barrage landed as Russians voted on the third and final day of a parliamentary election that Vladimir Putin has cast as a measure of support for the war. Sobyanin said the attack was planned to disrupt the vote, while Reuters reported election officials also said an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack.

Russia's defense ministry said its forces downed 1,110 Ukrainian drones across the country, over annexed Crimea and the Black Sea. Russia continued its own strikes on Ukraine in parallel, and Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, dismissed the Russian vote as a pseudo-election.

stories.whyItMatters: The scale of the strike shows Ukraine's long-range drone campaign now reaches Russia's political and economic core in single nights, and it landed deliberately on the one event the Kremlin is using to project domestic legitimacy.
stories.editorNote: The largest drone attack on Moscow of the war, on election day, is the single most consequential security event in today's feeds across BBC, Al Jazeera and Reuters.

stories.headline: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill
stories.dek: The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act targets Russian energy revenues and the shadow tanker fleet, and hands the president authority for tariffs of up to 100 percent on buyers of Russian oil and gas.
tldr: President Trump on Friday signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which passed the House 262-159 and the Senate 86-11.

The law targets Russia's energy and defense sectors and its shadow fleet of tankers, and requires duties of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian crude and gas, potentially including China and India.
The Kremlin said further US sanctions would make a peace deal in Ukraine harder to reach.

body.text: President Donald Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russian officials, banks and key sectors of the economy, the White House said on Friday. The measure, named for the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, is intended to deprive Moscow of the revenue funding its war in Ukraine.

The bill passed with large bipartisan margins, 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House, according to AP reporting carried by The Guardian. It sanctions Russian officials and banks, targets the shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving despite existing sanctions, and extends sanctions on Iran by five years.

The law also gives the president broad discretion over implementation, including authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that keep buying Russian oil and gas, potentially covering China and India. Democrats split over handing the White House that much trade power, AFP reported.

The signing follows a period in which the administration had been skeptical of new sanctions while mediated attempts to end the war stalled. The Kremlin said this week that additional US sanctions fall into the category of unfriendly actions and would make reaching a peace deal harder, according to The Moscow Times.

stories.whyItMatters: This converts months of congressional pressure into executable economic warfare, with secondary tariffs that could pull China and India into the sanctions standoff and reshape global oil flows.
stories.editorNote: The most significant escalation in the economic war on Russia since 2022, signed the same week Ukraine struck Russian refinery capacity, makes energy flows the central variable of the war.

stories.headline: Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control'
stories.dek: A US-Denmark-Greenland agreement promises Washington permanent access, basing and overflight rights while Copenhagen and Nuuk insist Danish sovereignty stays intact.
tldr: Trump announced a deal with Denmark and Greenland that he said gives the US 'permanent control over security' in Greenland, ending months of threats to take the island by force.
A State Department official said the agreement grants permanent access, basing and overflight rights, bans non-NATO bases and restricts investments by adversaries such as China and Russia.
Denmark and Greenland say the deal recognizes their sovereignty and self-determination; it is expected to be signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

body.text: President Trump announced on Friday that the United States has reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that he said gives Washington permanent control over security in the Arctic island. In a social media post, Trump said the US would immediately begin developing a larger military presence there, according to DW.

A State Department official told US media the deal guarantees permanent access, basing and overflight rights, bans any non-NATO military base in Greenland, and prevents China and Russia from establishing bases or making sensitive investments on the island.

Denmark and Greenland both welcomed the agreement, with Danish officials calling it good for NATO and Europe, but stressed it recognizes Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination. The deal is expected to be signed next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, and the precise scope of Trump's 'control' language remains unclear, Reuters reported.

stories.whyItMatters: The agreement settles, for now, a dispute that strained NATO's northern flank for two years, locking in an expanded US military footprint in the Arctic while formally keeping Greenland under Danish sovereignty.
stories.editorNote: A rare de-escalation in transatlantic friction with direct implications for Arctic basing and great-power competition, picked up across BBC, DW and The Guardian feeds.

stories.headline: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles
stories.dek: The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a missile over Riyadh after a fire at a fuel depot near the capital's airport, as Houthi attacks on Saudi territory sharply escalate.
tldr: The Houthis said they conducted two operations using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, targeting Riyadh and Aramco facilities in Yanbu, according to their military spokesman.
The Saudi-led coalition said air defenses intercepted a ballistic missile fired at Riyadh at dawn; a fire broke out at a fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport, an AFP journalist saw.
The escalation follows a Houthi ground offensive in Yemen and comes days after Saudi Arabia accused the group of targeting Mecca, which the Houthis deny.

body.text: Yemen's Houthi movement said it carried out two large-scale operations against Saudi Arabia, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying the first targeted what he described as sensitive sites in Riyadh and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Red Sea energy hub.

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh at dawn. An AFP journalist saw firefighters extinguish a blaze on a fuel tank bearing the Aramco logo at a depot near King Khalid International Airport, and flight tracking showed major disruption at the airport before traffic resumed.

The attack marks a sharp escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which has carried out scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas after the group's recent territorial offensive. DW's explainer assesses the group's current capabilities as the confrontation widens, and the US State Department issued a security alert warning the conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly.

stories.whyItMatters: Houthi missiles reaching Riyadh and Yanbu put Saudi energy infrastructure and the Red Sea corridor back in the crosshairs, with direct implications for oil markets and shipping.
stories.editorNote: Direct missile fire at the Saudi capital is a material supply-chain and chokepoint risk, and the BBC, DW and AFP coverage together map both the attack and the group's capabilities.

stories.headline: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
stories.dek: Voters go to the polls in two more states with the far-right AfD riding high after its landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, piling pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition and reform agenda.
tldr: Polls opened Sunday in further German state elections that will test Chancellor Friedrich Merz's standing after the AfD won 43.8 percent in Saxony-Anhalt this month, where his CDU fell to 17.2 percent.
Reuters reports Merz is under pressure as two more German states vote, with his pension and economic reforms unpopular and coalition stability in question.
Merz has ruled out cooperation with the AfD, whose rise he said will have repercussions on the international stage, including for policy toward Ukraine and Russia.

body.text: German state elections got under way Sunday in contests that could decide the political fate of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, the BBC reports, weeks after the far-right AfD's landslide in Saxony-Anhalt dealt his Christian Democrats a historic defeat.

In Saxony-Anhalt on 6 September the AfD took 43.8 percent of the vote to the CDU's 17.2 percent, coming within three seats of an absolute majority, according to projections and results reported by German media and Reuters. Merz said afterwards that the result changed not only Saxony-Anhalt but all of Germany.

Reuters reports Merz is under pressure as two more states go to the polls, with his government's pension reforms deeply unpopular in eastern Germany and his approval ratings down sharply. Merz has ruled out working with the AfD, whose politicians he notes maintain ties to Moscow and oppose support for Ukraine, and he said the AfD's rise would have repercussions on the international stage.

stories.whyItMatters: Germany is Europe's largest economy and Ukraine's second-largest backer; a further AfD surge narrows Berlin's room for continued military and fiscal support for Kyiv and destabilizes the EU's political center.
stories.editorNote: A second round of state voting in under three weeks makes this a live test of whether the Saxony-Anhalt earthquake was an outlier or a trend, with direct European security stakes.

stories.headline: Michelle Bachelet withdraws from race to become UN secretary general
stories.dek: The former Chilean president exited after a Security Council straw poll showed just one encourage vote, leaving seven candidates in the race to succeed Antonio Guterres.
tldr: Bachelet announced her withdrawal on Saturday after the Security Council's third informal straw poll, in which she received one encourage vote, 11 discourage votes and three no opinion votes, according to Al Jazeera.
She had placed second-to-last among eight candidates in the poll, which put Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan in the lead with nine encouraging votes.
Seven candidates remain for the post; Guterres's second term ends December 31, and no woman has ever held the position in the UN's history.

body.text: Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet announced on Saturday that she is withdrawing her candidacy to become the next UN secretary-general, saying she remained convinced her campaign had helped advance the case for a woman from Latin America to lead the organization.

Her exit followed the Security Council's third informal straw poll on Friday, in which she received one encourage vote, 11 discourage votes and three no opinion votes, finishing second-to-last among eight candidates, according to Al Jazeera. Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan led the first two polls, and Guyana's former foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett topped the third with eight encouraging votes.

Bachelet's campaign lost momentum after Chile's government withdrew its backing earlier this year. Seven candidates remain in the race to succeed Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, whose second term ends on December 31, with the Security Council due to recommend a single candidate to the General Assembly later this year.

stories.whyItMatters: The succession will define the UN's leadership through the end of the decade amid ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, and the straw-poll arithmetic shows the Security Council's permanent members are converging on a narrower field.
stories.editorNote: The clearest quantified datapoint in today's feed on who will next lead the UN, a selection with direct consequences for multilateral responses to every conflict covered above.
